For ease of use and code tidiness, we will use the unmerged datasets.


To visualize population distribution, we will combine the world dataset with the cities dataset. First, we will plot the countries, using a color gradient to show their total population. Then, we will overlay the cities, grouping them into seven size categories to highlight population concentration.



OECD classifies urban areas as:

large metropolitan areas if they have a population of 1.5 million or more;
metropolitan areas if their population is between 500 000 and 1.5 * million;
medium-size urban areas if their population is between 200 000 and 500 000; and,
small urban areas if their population is between 50 000 and 200 000.

We will also add two more categories:

Megacities (population greater than 10M)
Towns (population from 5k to 50k)
Villages (population lower than 5k)

Our categories are:

Very low (< 5k population)
Low (5k to 50k population)
Medium-Low (50k to 200k population)
Medium (200k to 500k population)
Medium-High (500k to 1.5M population)
High (1.5M to 10M population)
Very high (> 10M population)



Show the code
sf.cities <- sf.cities %>%
  mutate(pop_cat = cut( # creating categorical column for population
    pop,
    # Binning the population data
    breaks = c(- Inf, 5000, 50000, 200000, 500000, 
               1500000, 10000000, Inf),
    # Adding labels
    labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Medium-Low", "Medium", "Medium-High",
               "High", "Very high"),
    right = FALSE
  ))

st_drop_geometry(sf.cities) %>%
  count(pop_cat) # See if some categories do not contain many cities 


      pop_cat    n
1    Very Low  854
2         Low 2273
3  Medium-Low 2188
4      Medium 1020
5 Medium-High  702
6        High  286
7   Very high   19


The distribution of the cities looks okay, with very few cities in the “Very High” category (as expected). The NA’s are two very small cities present in the dataset which have negative population, which won’t affect our final analysis.



To keep the map readable, we will limit the number of cities shown for each country based on its size. Larger countries will show more cities, while smaller countries will show fewer


Show the code
# Auxiliary dataset
country_data <- sf.world %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  select(country, area_km2) # Keep only what we need

# Filtering cities based on Country Size
sf.cities.plot <- sf.cities %>%
  # Join the area data to the cities
  left_join(country_data, by = "country") %>%
  
  # Define the "City Limit" rules
  mutate(
    max_cities = case_when(
      area_km2 < 20000   ~ 1,
      area_km2 < 100000  ~ 3,
      area_km2 < 350000  ~ 6, 
      area_km2 < 1000000 ~ 10,
      area_km2 < 5000000 ~ 15,
      TRUE               ~ 25
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Applying the filter
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop)) %>%                # Sort largest to smallest
  filter(row_number() <= max_cities) %>% # Keep only the allowed amount
  ungroup()


Finally, we generate our plot.


Show the plotting code
# Plotting
ggplot() +
  
  # World map
  geom_sf(data = sf.world, aes(fill = pop), color = "white", size = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient( # gradient based on the country's population
    low = "#deebf7",
    high = "#08306b",
    name = "Country Pop", 
    trans = "log", # logarithmic scale so that the gradient is not completely skewed towards China and India
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()), # formatting the labels to make them more readable
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = 15, 
      barheight = 0.4,
      order = 1 
    )
  ) +
  
  guides(
    # Hiding shape and size legends
    shape = "none",
    size  = "none",
    
    # Keepig the color and putting title on Left
    color = guide_legend(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.vjust = 0.5, 
      nrow = 1, 
      order = 2)) + 

  # Cleaning
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + 
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    
    # Legend
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.margin = margin(t = 10, b = 10, l = 10, r = 10),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = -10, b = -10, l = 0, r = 0),
    
    # Image margins
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 0, l = 10, unit = "pt"),
    
    # Text styles
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold", color = "grey20"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6, color = "grey30"),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )









As a bonus, we can also visualize the world population map with the cities used to generate the population counts in each country, by their classifications:


Show the plotting code
# Defining custom shapes and colors
city_shapes <- c(
  "Very low" = 16, "Low" = 16, "Medium-Low" = 16, 
  "Medium" = 16, "Medium-High" = 16, "High" = 16, 
  "Very high" = 18 
)

city_colors <- c(
  "Very low"    = "#ffeda0",  
  "Low"         = "#feb24c",
  "Medium-Low"  = "#fd8d3c",
  "Medium"      = "#fc4e2a",
  "Medium-High" = "#e31a1c",
  "High"        = "#bd0026",
  "Very high"   = "#32cd32"
)

# Plotting
ggplot() +
  
  # World map
  geom_sf(data = sf.world, aes(fill = pop), color = "white", size = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient( # gradient based on the country's population
    low = "#deebf7",
    high = "#08306b",
    name = "Country Pop", 
    trans = "log10", # logarithmic scale so that the gradient is not completely skewed towards China and India
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()), # formatting the labels to make them more readable
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = 15, 
      barheight = 0.4,
      order = 1 
    )
  ) +
  
  # Cities
  geom_sf(
    data = sf.cities.plot %>% arrange(pop_cat), 
    aes(color = pop_cat, shape = pop_cat, size = pop_cat),
    alpha = 1
  ) +
  
  # Scales
  scale_shape_manual(values = city_shapes, name = "City Class") +
  scale_color_manual(values = city_colors, name = "City Class") +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 2), name = "City Class") +
  
  guides(
    # Hiding shape and size legends
    shape = "none",
    size  = "none",
    
    # Keepig the color and putting title on Left
    color = guide_legend(
      title.position = "left", 
      title.vjust = 0.5, 
      nrow = 1, 
      order = 2)) + 

  # Cleaning
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + 
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    
    # Legend
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.margin = margin(t = 10, b = 10, l = 10, r = 10),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = -10, b = -10, l = 0, r = 0),
    
    # Image margins
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 0, l = 10, unit = "pt"),
    
    # Text styles
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold", color = "grey20"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6, color = "grey30"),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )













Show the code
# Filter the data set to have only population and joint everything by country

sf.data_pop <- sf.data %>% 
  filter(type == 'CITY') %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  summarize(population = sum(pop))

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = population)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = '#08306b', fill = '#08519c') +
  labs(x = 'Population',
       y = 'Count', 
       title = 'World Population Distribution, by Country') +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = c("0", "100M", "200M", "300M"),
    breaks = c(0, 100000000, 200000000, 300000000)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+ 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))









Show the code
extremes <- sf.data_pop %>% 
  filter(population > 50000000)


Because the histogram with the current non-modified data is skewed to the left due to some extreme values from China, USA, India etc, we decided to compute the histogram applying a log scale to the population.


Show the code
# Compute the log of the population variable

sf.data_pop <- sf.data_pop %>%  
  mutate(log_pop = log(population))

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = log_pop)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = '#08306b', fill = '#08519c') +
  labs(x = 'Log Population',
       y = 'Count', 
       title = 'World Population Distribution, by Country (log scale)') +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))












To have a more detailed information on the population density we decided to compute the same log histograms for each of the continents.


Show the code
sf.data_pop <- sf.data_pop %>% 
  left_join(sf.world.aux %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(country, continent), 
            by = 'country')

ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = log_pop)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black') +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Population by Continent',
    x = 'Population',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )











Show the code
ggplot(sf.data_pop, aes(x = population)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black') +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Population by Continent',
    x = 'Population',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









By plotting the population distributions by continent without the log scale we clearly see exactly the same as before, there are some outliers in each continent that make the distribution skewed to the left.





Show the code
# Use data set sf.data
# Compute distance between cities and ports and airports by country
# Combine ports and airports
library(units)
sf.transport <- sf.data %>% filter(type %in% c('PORT', 'AIRPORT'))
sf.locations <- sf.data %>% filter(type == 'CITY')

# Calculate distance matrix to all transport hubs
distance_matrix <- st_distance(sf.locations$geom, sf.transport$geom)

# Get minimum distance for each city
sf.locations <- sf.locations %>%
  mutate(
    distance_to_nearest = apply(distance_matrix, 1, min), 
    distance_km = as.numeric(distance_to_nearest) / 1000   # Convert to km
  )

# Calculate country-level averages
country_distances <- sf.locations %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(country, continent) %>%
  summarize(avg_distance_km = mean(distance_km, na.rm = TRUE), 
            .groups = 'drop') %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent))




Show the plotting code
# plot
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = avg_distance_km)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









With the average distance in km for each continent, we cannot extract much information when we compare the distribution across continents. We take the log again.


Show the code
ggplot(country_distances, aes(x = log(avg_distance_km))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'black', alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = 'Log Distribution of Country Average Distances to Nearest Transport Hub',
    subtitle = 'Log Average distance from cities to nearest airport or port by continent',
    x = 'Log Average Distance',
    y = 'Number of Countries'
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust=0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40", hjust=0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









From the plots above using the log transformation, several insights can be highlighted. Africa shows higher average distances between cities and transport hubs compared to Europe, which may reflect less developed infrastructure, greater geographic dispersion of cities, or the continent’s larger land area. Europe and North America present similar distributions, with most countries clustered at lower average distances, suggesting well-developed and accessible transport networks.
South America shows less variability in average distances than Africa but centers around similar mean values, indicating moderate transport accessibility with less inter-country variation. Oceania, with fewer countries, exhibits high variability in average distances, likely due to the diverse geographic characteristics of island nations versus continental Australia. Asia displays the widest distribution, with many countries showing high average distances, potentially reflecting the continent’s vast size, varied development levels, and geographic diversity.

text:
Goals
Q1. Generate an sf POINT feature of marketplaces across Africa; plot them
Q2. Calculate minimum distance of each market to the (i) coast, (ii) nearest road, and (iii) nearest airport
Q3. Produce 3 scatter plots relating average prices with the minimum distances

Reference Paper:
Porteous, O., 2019. High trade costs and their consequences: An estimated dynamic model of African agricultural storage and trade. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 11(4), pp.327-66.
Direct link: Paper


Packages used:


Show the code
rm(list=ls())
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(spData)
library(osmdata)
library(readxl)
crumbs: Geospatial Data Science & Economic Spatial Models

title: Problem Set 2: Population & Marketplaces
text:
Data and sources
To complete this assignment, we will need data from several sources. First, we will use the spData library, which contains the world shapefile. In addition, we will need datasets for roads, highways, airports, and the coastline, as well as data from the replication paper that features marketplaces across Africa.
Sources:

Airports
Highways and Roads
Coastline
Market Locations and Prices


Loading the Data
First we create a polygon from the world shape file in spData so we can use it to filter through intersections with other datasets


Show the code
africa <- world %>%  filter(continent == "Africa")

africa_poly <- africa %>% 
  summarise(geom = st_union(geom), .groups = "drop")


We load the different shapefiles for the roads, the coastline and the airports:


Show the code
africa_roads_raw<-st_read("Data/groads-v1-africa-shp/gROADS-v1-africa.shp", quiet = TRUE) #Roads data

africa_roads_clean<- africa_roads_raw %>%
  filter(LENGTH_KM >= 20) %>%
  st_crop(africa_poly) %>%              
  st_intersection(africa_poly)  

coastline<-st_read("Data/ne_10m_coastline/ne_10m_coastline.shp", quiet = TRUE)
coastline_africa <- st_intersection(coastline, africa)



airports<-st_read("Data/ne_10m_airports/ne_10m_airports.shp", quiet = TRUE)
airports_africa  <- st_intersection(airports, africa)


For the Africa roads layer, we apply two filters. First, we keep only roads with LENGTH_KM >= 20 so that smaller roads are not considered. We choose this for a couple of reasons; first, because computationally it is very expensive to compute intersections and distances for over 500k+ road observations, so reducing the size of this dataset is beneficial to the efficiency of our task execution; second, because this is a much more relevant analysis of the data – we care more about the distance a market has to a more important, well-connected road than it does to some random neighborhood or back road that may only spans one kilometer and connects to very few homes.
Second, we clip the roads to the Africa polygon (africa_poly) derived from the world dataset, because the roads shapefile also includes features from the Middle East and the southern part of Europe. We use st_intersection() for an exact spatial clip to Africa and we apply the same concept to the coastline data and the airports data.

coords <- read_excel("Data/markets/MktCoords.xlsx", sheet = "MarketCoordinates")

# 2) Convert to sf points

title: Problem Set 2: Population & Marketplaces
text:
Q2.2: Calculate Min Distances
We can combine what we have obtained before with the roads data to obtain the following plot:


Show the code
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = africa_roads_clean, aes(color = "Roads"), 
          linewidth = 0.3, key_glyph = draw_key_path) +
  geom_sf(data = mkt_pts, aes(color = "Markets"), size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Markets" = "red",
      "Roads"   = "grey30"
    ),
    breaks = c("Markets", "Roads")
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linewidth = c(0, 1),
        shape     = c(16, NA),
        size      = c(3, 0)
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Roads and Markets in Africa") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5)
  )









And combine the previous plot with the the coast and airport data:


Show the code
ggplot() +
  # Africa background
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +

  # Roads
  geom_sf(
    data = africa_roads_clean,
    aes(color = "Roads"),
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.6,
    key_glyph = draw_key_path
  ) +

  # Coastline
  geom_sf(
    data = coastline_africa,
    aes(color = "Coastline"),
    linewidth = 0.4,
    key_glyph = draw_key_path
  ) +

  # Airports
  geom_sf(
    data = airports_africa,
    aes(color = "Airports"),
    size = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +

  # Market points
  geom_sf(
    data = mkt_pts,
    aes(color = "Markets"),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Roads"     = "grey30",
      "Coastline" = "purple",
      "Airports"  = "#1f78b4",
      "Markets"   = "red"
    ),
    breaks = c("Markets", "Airports", "Roads", "Coastline")
  ) +
  
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linewidth = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
        shape     = c(16, 16, NA, NA),
        size      = c(3, 3, 0, 0),
        alpha     = c(1, 1, 1, 1)
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Infrastructure and Markets in Africa") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5)
  )










Computing the distances
To compute the minimum distance:


Show the code
# Nearest feature index for each market
idx_coast   <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, coastline_africa)
idx_road    <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, africa_roads_clean)
idx_airport <- st_nearest_feature(mkt_pts, airports_africa)


We want the minimum distance for each market individually and we want to compute it efficiently and correctly, without building a huge distance matrix or mixing markets together, st_nearest_feature() tells us which feature is the closest one to each market.
Then we compute the distance only to that feature:


Show the code
# Minimum distance (meters) to the nearest feature (by element)
d_coast_m <- st_distance(mkt_pts, coastline_africa[idx_coast, ], by_element = TRUE)
d_road_m  <- st_distance(mkt_pts, africa_roads_clean[idx_road, ],      by_element = TRUE)
d_air_m   <- st_distance(mkt_pts, airports_africa[idx_airport,], by_element = TRUE)

# Attach to the markets table (convert to numeric km)
mkt_pts <- mkt_pts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_coast_km   = as.numeric(d_coast_m) / 1000,
    dist_road_km    = as.numeric(d_road_m)  / 1000,
    dist_airport_km = as.numeric(d_air_m)   / 1000
  )


For each market location, we compute the minimum Euclidean distance to the three types of spatial infrastructure: the coastline, the road network, and the nearest airport. This is done using the st_distance() function.
Before computing distances, each market is matched to its nearest feature of the relevant type (coast, road, or airport). Using these matches, st_distance() is applied with the option by_element = TRUE, which ensures that distances are calculated pairwise, which makes that each market is compared only to its own nearest feature rather than to all features in the dataset. As a result, the output is a vector of minimum distances, one value per market, expressed in meters, which correspond to the coordinate reference system of the spatial data.
The resulting distance vectors are then added to the markets dataset as new variables. Distances are converted from meters to kilometers by dividing by 1,000 and stored in three different variables: distance to the coast, distance to the nearest road, and distance to the nearest airport.
We can check the mean distances for each of the three variables:


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_coast_km)


     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
   0.1478  178.1537  530.0659  571.5270  925.7852 1736.1293 


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_road_km)


     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
7.255e-03 9.458e-01 3.044e+00 1.165e+01 1.069e+01 1.238e+02 


Show the code
summary(mkt_pts$dist_airport_km)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.11   24.30  201.73  229.19  338.24  915.61 


It can be seen that each variable has very different interpretation as its values vary deeply:

Distance to coast: On average, markets are located about 572km from the coastline, indicating that many markets are substantially inland.
Distance to roads: Markets are, on average, about 11.7km away from the nearest major road, suggesting relatively good road accessibility (We have to consider the filter of minimum 20km length applied in the beginning for the roads for this interpretation, which means that if the filter was not applied we could expect a lower distance on average).
Distance to airports: The average distance to the nearest airport is approximately 229km, implying limited proximity to air transport infrastructure for most markets.

We could also inspect an specific market row:


Show the code
i <- 5  # pick a market row to inspect

# ggplot() +
#   geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
#   geom_sf(data = coastline_africa, color = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
#   geom_sf(data = africa_roads_clean, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = coastline_africa, aes(color = "Coastline"), 
          linewidth = 0.3, key_glyph = draw_key_path) +
  geom_sf(data = africa_roads_clean, aes(color = "Roads"), 
          linewidth = 0.3, key_glyph = draw_key_path) +
  geom_sf(data = airports_africa, aes(color = "Other Airports"), size = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = mkt_pts[i,], aes(color = "Selected Market"), size = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = airports_africa[idx_airport[i],], aes(color = "Nearest Airport"), size = 4, shape = 17) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Coastline"       = "purple",
      "Roads"           = "grey30",
      "Other Airports"  = "#1f78b4",
      "Selected Market" = "red",
      "Nearest Airport" = "gold"
    ),
    breaks = c("Selected Market", "Nearest Airport", 
               "Other Airports", "Roads", "Coastline")
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linewidth = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1),
        size      = c(3, 3, 3, 0, 0),      
        shape     = c(16, 17, 16, NA, NA)  
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Closest Airport to a Select Market") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









We can also construct lines to see the distance:


Show the code
lines_airport <- st_nearest_points(
  mkt_pts,
  airports_africa[idx_airport, ],
  pairwise = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf()

lines_coast <- st_nearest_points(
  mkt_pts,
  coastline_africa[idx_coast, ],
  pairwise = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf()

lines_road <- st_nearest_points(
  mkt_pts,
  africa_roads_clean[idx_road, ],
  pairwise = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf()


We construct LINESTRING geometries representing the minimum (nearest-neighbor) distance from each market location to key infrastructure features. Using st_nearest_points(), we connect each market to its closest airport, coastline, and road segment.
We can plot this:


Show the code
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, fill = "grey95", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  
  geom_sf(data = lines_coast,   aes(color = "Distance to Coast"), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = lines_road,    aes(color = "Distance to Road"),  linewidth = 0.4) +

  geom_sf(data = airports_africa, aes(color = "Airport"), size = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = mkt_pts,         aes(color = "Market"),  size = 2) +

    name = "Legend",

      "Airport"             = "blue",
      "Distance to Coast"   = "black",
      "Distance to Road"    = "green",
      "Distance to Airport" = "#1f78b4"
      )
    ) +
  labs(title = "Distance between Markets and Closest Infrastructure") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),

  )

Q2.3: Scatterplots

Constructing and merging the data
First, we obtain the price data from the replication package and compute, for each market, the average price across all time periods and across all crops. The raw price data contain multiple columns corresponding to different time periods. Some observations contain many NA or 0 values, for which we convert all to NA and calculate the average price over all available time periods.


Show the code
# import dataset from excel sheet
prices_raw <- read_excel("Data/markets/MktPrices.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")

# extract all the numeric column names (prices)
price_cols <- names(prices_raw)[grep("^\\d+$", names(prices_raw))]

avg_prices <- prices_raw %>%  
  mutate(
    across(all_of(price_cols), ~ na_if(., 0)),
    price = rowMeans(pick(all_of(price_cols)), na.rm=T)
    ) %>% 
  group_by(mktcode) %>% 
  summarize(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm=T))


Once we have obtained the average values we can merge the two datasets by mktcode


Show the code
mkt_pts <- mkt_pts %>%
  left_join(avg_prices, by = "mktcode")




Constructing the plots
We construct three scatter plots relating average market prices to the minimum distance to the coast, the nearest road, and the nearest airport.

Average Prices vs Distance to Coast

# load in libraries
rm(list=ls())
library(terra)         # raster operations
library(exactextractr) # exact_extract() for distances

library(sf)            # vector operations

library(tidyverse)     # NOTE: Conflict -- tidyr::extract() masks terra::extract()
library(glue)          # printf() syntax
library(spDataLarge)   # geo data
library(ggrepel)       # add labels to ggplot
library(tidyterra)     # visualize geospatial using tidy syntax
library(patchwork)     # patch tg ggplot objects


# load in data
load("C:/Users/T14/7Programming/R/class/geospatial/notes/07/data_for_class09.rdata")


# initial visualization of grid
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=grid) +
  geom_sf(data=routes) +
  theme_void()


## extract long/lat from each grid
df <- data.frame(latitude = grid$latitude, 
                 longitude = grid$longitude)

# convert to simple feature multipoint object
sf.cities <- st_as_sf(df,
                      coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'),
                      crs = 'EPSG:4326')
# updated plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=grid) +
  geom_sf(data=routes) +
  geom_sf(data=sf.cities) +
  theme_void()


# calculate paths between cities using routes
r.template <- rast()
values(r.template) <- runif(1:ncell(r.template))

# crop to spain bounds
r.template <- terra::crop(r.template, grid)

# sanity check
plot(r.template)


res(r.template) <- 0.01                # set res to much finer for more precision
values(r.template) <- runif(1:ncell(r.template))

# sanity check
plot(r.template)
plot(st_geometry(grid), add=T, col=adjustcolor("gray", alpha.f=0.35))


r.routes <- terra::rasterize(x=routes,         # vector object
                            y=r.template,  # template raster
                            field = 1)     # optional: set touching vals = 1

# cells on the network = 1, off-network = NA
plot(r.routes, main = "Rasterized Gridcell Map")
plot(st_geometry(grid), add = TRUE) 


# convert NA values to 0 to compute distances later on
r.routes_filled <- r.routes
r.routes_filled[is.na(r.routes_filled)] <- 0 # replace NA values with 0

# convert: SpatRaster -> RasterLayer
r.routes_filled <- raster::raster(r.routes_filled)

# transition matrix
trans <- gdistance::transition(
  x = r.routes_filled,             # must be a gdistance::RasterLayer object
  transitionFunction = mean,   
  directions = 8                  # max 8-gridcells surrounding any given gridcell
)


trans_corrected <- geoCorrection(trans, type = "c")


city_geoms <- sf.cities                               # extract city geoms
num_cities <- dim(sf.cities)[1]                       # num of cities
city_paths <- list()                                  # init empty list to store paths
city_pairs <- matrix(0, 
                     nrow = num_cities,
                     ncol = num_cities)

for (i in 1:(num_cities - 1)) {
  for (j in (i + 1):num_cities) {
    
    origin_sp <- as(city_geoms[i, ], "Spatial")
    goal_sp   <- as(city_geoms[j, ], "Spatial")
    
    path <- gdistance::shortestPath(
      x      = trans_corrected,
      origin = origin_sp,
      goal   = goal_sp,
      output = "SpatialLines"
    )
    
    dist <- SpatialLinesLengths(path, longlat = TRUE)
    city_pairs[i, j] <- dist
    city_pairs[j, i] <- dist  # symmetric
    
  }
}

# table results
city_pairs


# compute market access: sum of: { pop * e^(distance(i,j) * 0.001) } for every city
MA_list = c() # init empty list of MA values for each city 1-72
pops <- grid$pop.2000
theta = 6.5

for (i in 1:num_cities){
  scaled_dists <- city_pairs[i, ] * 0.001
  MA_list[i] <- sum(pops * exp(-theta * scaled_dists))
}

# assign values back into grid vector object
grid$MA <- MA_list
grid # sanity check


# rescale to [0,1] for plotting purposes
grid$MA_scaled <- scales::rescale(grid$MA, to = c(0, 1))
# plot MA by gridcell
ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data=grid, aes(fill=MA_scaled))+
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name   = "Market Access",
    option = "H",        # try "magma", "inferno", "cividis", "turbo"
    limits = c(0, 1))+
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position   = "right",
    legend.direction  = "vertical",
    legend.title      = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    legend.text       = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.width  = unit(0.3, "cm"),   # skinny bar
    legend.key.height = unit(1.5, "cm")
    )

title: Class 05: Raster-Vector Operations
text:
Loading
Using the terra::rast() function, we can load raster data from downloaded sources. Note that raster data has two main formats:

‘.tif’ (most common)
‘.nc’ (multilayer)


.tif






Note



Nightlight data is downloaded from Earth Observation Group, specifically annual VNL V2.2, since it contains consistently processed annual composites, covering 2012 to present. We selected the ‘average-masked’ values, as it helps to filter out edge cases such as fires and diurnal lighting.



r.nlights <- rast('nightlights/NL.tif')

inMemory(r.nlights) #note: not loaded in memory!

Note that raster data is not stored in memory. This is extremely important data management as raster data files can be huge (the NL.tif file is >10gb!)
To deal with this specific nightlight data properly, note that since majority of the world is dark at night (think the ocean, deserts, seas, etc), we need to rescale our data as majority of the observations (gridcells) are zero-valued;

summary(r.nlights)
hist(r.nlights, maxcell = 1e6) # heavy left-skew; need to rescale

r.log <- log1p(r.nlights)  # log1p: log(1+x) rescales well for majority zero-val obs

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(r.nlights, main = "pre-processed") # note the majority purple map
plot(r.log, main = "processed using log(1+x)")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))



.nc
Multilayer format: NETCDF .nc

r.spei <- rast("data/spei01.nc")
r.spei

Note the values for nlyr – these are our “layers”; 1380 in this case corresponds to each time unit – the data is monthly, spanning from January 1901 to January 2015, resulting in 1380 total months.
We will blow up the graph if we do not explicitly select a sub layer! To do so, we must subset by a unit index (or alternatively by name, if the indices are labeled, given as ‘names’)


Code
glue("the associated names for the 'spei.nc' layers: '{paste(head(names(r.spei), n=4), collapse = ', ')}' ...")

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(r.spei[[1]], main="index: 't=1'") # note the [[x]] -- returns layer x as a spatRaster object
plot(r.spei[['spei_10']], main="index: 't=10'")
plot(r.spei[[15]], main="index: 't=15'")
plot(r.spei[['spei_21']], main="index: 't=21'")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))








Note



The SPEI data is used to monitor global droughts, given as monthly data updated at the first days of each subsequent month, built according to global temperature indices and global precipitation sums.

title: Class 05: Raster-Vector Operations
text:
Extraction
Extracting the raster value from each cell, where the vertices of a vector object is overlaying the cells. In other words, we care about the intersection of a vector object onto the gridcells of a raster object. sf_multipoints return a value for each cell it is contained within; sf_polygon returns one value for each vertex.

Points
For example, let us look at the Zion example from last class.

 # raster: meters above sea lvl
r.srtm = rast(system.file("raster/srtm.tif", 
                          package = "spDataLarge"))

# vector: 30 random data points from Zion
sf.zion_pts <- spDataLarge::zion_points 
sf.zion_pts

Note that we have a raster object and vector object both loaded into our environment now. To extract the values at which the sf.zion_pts vector values intersect with the r.srtm gridcells, we use the terra::extract() function to return a dataFrame, where each vector point has its associated gridcell value mapped to it:

# extract()
elevation = terra::extract(r.srtm, sf.zion_pts) # 30x2 df: extract elevation from each zion pt
head(elevation)







Note



Note that the terra::extract function works sequentially row-wise; it starts from the first observation from the vector object, extract the intersecting gridcell value from the associated raster object, then returns the row number as an “ID” column and the gridcell value as its own column.


Note we can use the cbind() function to now bind these elevation values back to our sf.zion_pts vector object

# cbind()
sf.zion_pts = cbind(sf.zion_pts, elevation)  
sf.zion_pts







Warning



We can do the same for sf_linestrings, however, it is not recommended to obtain values along the transect, as it is difficult to get correct distances between each pair of extracted values. The reason is that a linestring may move diagonally and intersect multiple gridcells at a time, given a sort of ‘staircase effect.’ Further, if a line runs through mostly one gridcell and barely clips the corner of another, they are treated equally and both filled in.




Linestrings
It is recommended to break up the linestring into multipoints and then extract the values from these points to avoid any issues with distances. For example, imagine we are planning a hike through Zion and want to know the elevation change as we travel along this line.

# create a linestring object for dmeo
sf.zion_transect = cbind(c(-113.2, -112.9), c(37.45, 37.2)) |>
  st_linestring() |> 
  st_sfc(crs = crs(r.srtm)) |>
  st_sf(geometry = _)

First, we must create an unique ID for each row in the object. Afterwards, we then assign equal points along this linestring using the st_segmentize() function from sf, as specify a given density.

sf.zion_transect$id = 1:nrow(sf.zion_transect) 
sf.zion_transect = st_segmentize(sf.zion_transect, dfMaxLength = 250) # add points
sf.zion_transect

Finally, we use st_cast() to convert these segmented points into sf_multipoint objects.

sf.zion_transect = st_cast(sf.zion_transect, "POINT")
head(sf.zion_transect)

Now, with a large set of points along our line segment, we want to calculate distances between the first point (starting pt) and any subsequent pts using st_distance() after grouping by ID (since they all share the same ID value, even after casting).

# distance from starting pt
sf.zion_transect = sf.zion_transect |> 
  group_by(id) |> 
  mutate(dist = st_distance(geometry)[, 1]) 
head(sf.zion_transect) # sanity check

Finally, we can use terra::extract() to retrieve the associated elevation (raster gridcell values) that intersect each vector point, and bind this back to our linestring vector object to get our results.

# extract value of elevation gridcells where vector points intersect
df.zion_elev = terra::extract(r.srtm, sf.zion_transect)
# append back to our original object
sf.zion_transect = cbind(sf.zion_transect, df.zion_elev)
head(sf.zion_transect)



Code
sf.zion <- read_sf(system.file("vector/zion.gpkg", package = "spDataLarge")) # zion ntl park

p1<- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=r.srtm) +
  geom_sf(data=sf.zion, fill=NA,
          lwd=0.7, col="black")+
  geom_sf(data=sf.zion_transect) +
  # Black outlines
  geom_sf(data = filter(sf.zion_transect, dist == min(dist) | dist == max(dist)),
          shape = 23, color = "black", fill = NA, size = 4.5, stroke = 1) +
  # Colored centers
  geom_sf(data = filter(sf.zion_transect, dist == min(dist)),
          shape = 23, color = "black", fill = "blue", size = 4) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(sf.zion_transect, dist == max(dist)),
          shape = 23, color = "black", fill = "red", size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = filter(sf.zion_transect, 
                          dist == min(dist) | dist == max(dist)),
            aes(label = if_else(dist == min(dist), 
                                "start", 
                                "end"),
                geometry = geometry),
            vjust = -1,
            stat = "sf_coordinates",
            hjust = 0.113)+
  scale_fill_terrain_c(guide = guide_colorbar(
      title.position = "top", 
      title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = 0.5, 
      barheight = 15,
      order = 1  
    )) +
  labs(title = "Hike through Zion",
       fill = "Elevation [m]") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))

  
p2<- ggplot(data=st_drop_geometry(sf.zion_transect),
            aes(x=as.double(dist), y=srtm))+
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Elevation Change",
       x = "Distance [m]", 
       y = "Elevation [m]")+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))
  
  
p1+p2




Polygons






Note



Here, we are using the exactextractr::exact_extract() function, as it is computationally efficient; if we want more precise raster values (at the cost of more computational power), we would use terra::extract(). Note that this exact_extract() operation requires standardization from a sf vector into SpatVec().
By default, exact_extract() calculates the fraction of each cell covered by the polygon, which is much more precise; this way, we can deal more appropriately with cells that are mostly covered by a point versus cells that barely touch.



Zonal Statistics
As mentioned previously, polygons return values for each vertex that intersects a gridcell. Such results can be used to generate summary statistics for raster values per polygon, for example to characterize a single region or to compare many regions.

# note that exact_extract does NOT create an ID column
zion_srtm_values <- exactextractr::exact_extract(x = r.srtm, 
                                                   y = sf.zion)
zion_srtm_values <- zion_srtm_values[[1]]

zion_srtm_values %>%                  #summary stats
  rename(elevation = value) %>% 
    summarize(across(elevation, 
                     list(min = min, 
                          mean = mean, 
                          max = max)))

We can also get the zonal statistics of overlaying raster values in a polygon directly by using the fun argument in the exact_extract() function; for example,

zion.zonal <- exact_extract(x=r.srtm,      # raster
                            y= sf.zion,    # polygon 
                            fun = c('mean', 'min', 'max'))  # statistic: min/max/mean/sum, etc
glue("average elevation in Zion national park: {round(zion.zonal$mean,2)} [m]
     minimum elevation in Zion national park: {round(zion.zonal$min,2)} [m]
     maximum elevation in Zion national park: {round(zion.zonal$max,2)} [m]")

Because there is only one polygon in the example, a data frame with a single row is returned; however, the method works when multiple selector polygons are used.
A similar approach works for counting occurrences of categorical raster values within polygons.

r.nlcd = rast(system.file("raster/nlcd.tif", 
                          package = "spDataLarge"))
r.nlcd_labels <- levels(r.nlcd)[[1]]

sf.zion2 = st_transform(sf.zion, st_crs(r.nlcd))

df.zion_nlcd<-exact_extract(r.nlcd, sf.zion2)[[1]]

df.zion_nlcd %>% 
  group_by(value) %>% 
  count() %>% 
  left_join(r.nlcd_labels, by = "value") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  select(levels, n)



Code
# Continuous Data (SRTM)
p_srtm <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r.srtm) +
  geom_sf(data = sf.zion, fill = "gray", alpha=0.35,
          color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_terrain_c() +
  labs(title = "A. Continuous data extraction", fill = "Elevation (m)") +
  theme_void() + # Or theme_minimal()
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = c(0.18, 0.19), 
    legend.direction = "vertical",
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black"),
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold")
  )

nlcd_colors <- c(
  "Water" = "#466b9f", 
  "Developed" = "#d83121", 
  "Barren" = "#af968c", 
  "Forest" = "#308e51", 
  "Shrubland" = "#ccba7d", 
  "Herbaceous" = "#e3e3c2", 
  "Cultivated" = "#dbd83d", 
  "Wetlands" = "#70a3ba",
  "NA" = "transparent"
)

# Categorical Data (NLCD)
p_nlcd <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r.nlcd) +
  geom_sf(data = sf.zion2, fill = "gray", alpha = 0.35,
          color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Using a dedicated "wiki" palette for distinct land cover colors
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = nlcd_colors,
    na.translate = FALSE,
    guide = guide_legend(
      title = "Land Cover",
      nrow = 3, 
      byrow = TRUE,
      override.aes = list(size = 4) # Makes legend boxes bigger/easier to see
    )

title: Class 05: Raster-Vector Operations
text:
Rasterization
Rasterizing sf vector data: transform a vector object into a raster object. Works by assigning non-missing values for the intersection raster grid cells (pixels); otherwise, leaves missing.
Very computationally demanding; only has one realistic (but powerful) use case: distances over friction surfaces
Intuition: distances between two ports over the seine river. Vector operations would “cheat” and find the shortest path on the 2D euclidean plane; raster objects must follow the path given by non-NA gridcells.


Code
sf.seine <- spData::seine



ggplot(data=sf.seine)+
  geom_sf(aes(color=name),
          lwd=0.7) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = name,
                   color = name),
               hjust=2,
               fontface = "italic", 
               size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Rivers of the Seine")+
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title=element_text(hjust=0.5),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
        legend.position = 'none')



Calculating Distances: step-by-step

rasterize()

Rasterize the vector using rasterize()

To do so, we need to objects: the vector object we wish to convert, and a ‘raster template.’ To create an appropriate raster template, we simple initialize a rast() object and crop it to the bounds of our vector object.

Note: We must make sure our projections align; any time we initialize a rast() object, it by default takes on WGS84 projection. Thus, if our vector object has a different projection, we will get an error when trying to initialize the raster template.


r.template <- rast() %>% 
  crop(sf.seine) # Watch out for the projections!


sf.seine <- sf.seine %>% 
  st_transform('EPSG:4326')

sf.seine

r.template <- rast() %>% # our cropped raster template
  crop(sf.seine)

Then, we can apply the terra::rasterize() function:

r.seine <- terra::rasterize(x=sf.seine,    # vector object
                            y=r.template,  # template raster
                            field = 1)     # optional: set touching vals = 1

# cells on the network = 1, off-network = NA
plot(r.seine, main = "Rasterized Seine network")
plot(sf.seine, add = TRUE, col = "blue") 

Note that we have low resolution! With a size of \(3 \times 5\) with \(1^o \times 1^o\) resolution means we only have 15 gridcells! Thus, our sf.seine object intersects nearly the entire raster template; to make this more precise, we need to adjust the resolution of our raster template object and re-rasterize.

r.seine

res(r.template) <- .05
r.template               # new res increased size to 60x100 = 6,000 gridcells!

With an exponential increase in resolution, we can get a more detailed rasterized object:

r.seine <- rasterize(x = sf.seine,
                     y= r.template,
                     field = 1)
# cells on the network = 1, off-network = NA
plot(r.seine, main = "Rasterized Seine network")
plot(sf.seine, add = TRUE, col = "blue") 



transition()

gdistance::transition()

First, we must convert the NA values to become 0. That way, any distance operations do not fail (when we pass NA) and only matter for non-zero integers. We do this using the is.na() function called onto our newly rasterized r.seine object.

r.seine_filled <- r.seine
r.seine_filled[is.na(r.seine_filled)] <- 0 # replace NA values with 0

After which we build a transition() matrix – think of each raster cell as a node in a network graph. transition() looks at every pair of neighboring cells and asks: “how easy is it to move between these two cells?” The answer gets stored as an edge weight in a large sparse matrix: one row/column per cell, with values representing the cost or ease of traversal.
Another way to think of a transition matrix is a sparse matrix we store network data in to represent graphs (networks) as a matrix to perform calculations on.

r.seine_filled <- raster::raster(r.seine_filled) # convert: SpatRaster --> RasterLayer

# mean conductance between neighbors; 8 directions of movement
trans <- gdistance::transition(
  x = r.seine_filled,          # must be a gsitance::Rasterlayer object (not terra::SpatRaster)
  transitionFunction = mean,   # average conductance of two neighboring cells
  directions = 8               # 8-connected (includes diagonals)
)







Note



Note some of the arguments included in the transition() function








Argument | Function | Values | ===========+===========+====================+ x | passes the raster object to be transitioned into a matrix | - RasterLayer |


transitionFunction | When deciding the cost of moving from cell A to cell B, it takes the average conductance of both cells. If one cell is 0 (off-network) and the other is 1 (on-network), the mean is 0.5 — a partial barrier. If both are 0, mean is 0: completely impassable. If both are 1, mean is 1: free movement. This is what keeps the path constrained to the river network. | - mean | | |


directions | Specifies which directions each cell can ‘see’ – think of number of sides of a shape; 4 represents a square, 8 a octagon, 16, etc. Note we selection 8 since there are 8 gridcells at most surrounding any given gridcell | - 4 (cardinal NWSE) | | | - 8 (N NW W SW S SE E NE) |



Note that after we build the matrix, we must correct for diagonal distances, as in a grid, the distance between two horizontally or vertically adjacent cells is 1 cell width. But the distance between two diagonally adjacent cells is \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\) cell widths. Without correction, the algorithm treats both as equal cost.

# correct for diagonal distances (geometric correction)
trans_corrected <- geoCorrection(trans, type = "c")







Important



Without geoCorrection(), a path that moves diagonally across 10 cells would appear to cost the same as one moving cardinally across 10 cells, even though the diagonal path is actually $ 41%$ longer in real space. This means the algorithm would prefer diagonal movement, producing paths that snake diagonally rather than following the true network geometry. The correction scales each edge weight by the actual geographic distance between cell centers.




shortestpath()

gdistance::shortestpath() employs a ‘minimum-cost’ (Dijkstra) pathfinding algorithm

Importantly, we must select a start and end point in our raster object for the algorithm to calculate the shortest path between.






Important



if you place a point in a cell with value 0 (off-network), the algorithm either fails or snaps to the nearest network cell in an unpredictable way.


To employ, our function needs four arguments:







Argument
x
Function | Inputs | ===========+====================+ passes the TransitionLayer matrix in | - TransitionLayer | | |




origin
starting cell | - SpatialPoints(matrix(coords)) | | - as_Spatial(sf.points[x1,]) |


goal
destination cell | - SpatialPoints(matrix(coords)) | | - as_Spatial(sf.points[x2,]) |


output
controls the format the result comes back in a drawable line connecting the two points, or investigate the individual cells the path traversed along | - “SpatialLines” (default) | - “SpatialPixels” |




# Good practice: sample directly from the vector network

# get all coordinates for vector object
coords    <- st_coordinates(sf.seine)
coords_sp <- SpatialPoints(coords[, 1:2])

# get coords for all raster gridcells
network_vals <- terra::extract(r.seine_filled, coords_sp)

# only keep coords that contained in raster gridcells (also deal with NAs)
valid_coords <- coords[network_vals %in% 1, ] 

origin      <- SpatialPoints(matrix(valid_coords[1, 1:2], ncol = 2))
destination <- SpatialPoints(matrix(valid_coords[nrow(valid_coords), 1:2], ncol = 2))


# shortest path algorithm
path <- shortestPath(
  x      = trans_corrected,
  origin = origin,
  goal   = destination,
  output = "SpatialLines"
)

plot(r.seine, col="pink", 
     legend   = FALSE,         # remove the legend
     axes     = FALSE,         # remove axis labels and gridlines
     main = "Rasterized Seine network w/ Shortest Path")
plot(path, add=T,
     col ="blue", lwd=2)

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Main reference for these notes is Lovelace, R., Nowosad, J. and Muenchow, J., 2019. Geocomputation with R. Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://r.geocompx.org/geometry-operations
This chapter, quote: “…focuses on manipulating the geographic elements of spatial objects.” This includes:

Simplification: reducing memory size by reducing geometries
Centroids: calculating the center of mass of a geometry object
Buffers: generate buffer zones surrounding a geometry
Casting: transform between geometry types
Clipping: restricting geometry space b/w two objects
Distances: calculating distance b/w one or two geometry objects
Transformations: shifting, scaling, and rotations

style=“color:blue”>Geometry Operations are manipulations of vector data that manipulates its geometry.
Here are the main libraries we will use for these notes:

library(sf)           # simple-features library
library(terra)        # spatial data analysis
library(tidyverse)    # tidyverse: data manipulation, ggplot
library(spData)       # gives us example spatial datasets
library(spDataLarge)  # gives us example large spatial datasets
library(patchwork)    # put ggplots side-by-side
library(rmapshaper)   # for ms_simplify()
library(smoothr)      # for smooth()
crumbs: Geospatial Data Science & Economic Spatial Models

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Motivation: Coastline Paradox
Let’s say you’re trying to measure the length of coastline of a nation, say Iceland. Further, imagine that we are measuring the coastline using a 500km ruler. The resulting measurement will be quite inaccurate, much lower than the true coastline length since we cannot account for small edges and turns.
Then, we use a 100km ruler to measure the coastline and obtain a new measurement, which is still inaccurate, but our measured coastline value has now increased as our margin of error decreases as we are able to account for more details of the curves around the coastline.
Now imagine this measurement process iteratively:
500km -> 100km -> 10km -> 1km -> …. -> tracing around every pebble and grain of sand -> … -> tracing around every Planck length of matter.
What do we think happens to the value we obtain for the coastline?
Essentially, the length of our coastline approaches infinity as our our measurement device records smaller and smaller values. This result is obviously impossible, since the length of a coastline has to be a finite value. Thus, we arrive at the Coastline Paradox, first noted by Lewis Fry Richardson in the 1920s.






500km Ruler Measurement: 3000km







100km Ruler Measurement: 4000km







1km Ruler Measurement: 4500km





Put in more formal terms, where \(n\) is the length of our measurement device, and the function \(f(n) = \frac{1}{n}\) gives us the basic inverse relationship between coastline length and length of measurement device:
\[
\lim_{n \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{n} = \infty
\]






Inverse Relationship between Length of Coastline & Length of Measurement Device





The reason for this phenomena is fractals: if we start very zoomed out, everything looks quite “smooth”, and we see the outline of bays and peninsulas. As we zoom in further, we see that each bay as its own inlet; even further, that each inlet has rocky shorelines; further, each individual rock has crevices; sand grains have irregular edges; and so forth.












Fractals











Theoretically, our measurement devices are capable of approaching measuring lengths \(\rightarrow 0\). However, in reality this is not possible nor feasible; as some point, the measurements would flatten enough where even smaller measurements would not affect the length of the coastline at some significance level. Further, it not physically possible to create measuring devices of such a microscopic scale.
What does this paradox have to do with our geospatial data?
When computing spatial geometries, these types of geometries & their associated calculations can take up a lot of memory in exchange for very precise maps. Thus, we might want to take a extremely precise map, measured with very ‘small’ measuring sticks, and scale it back to a more inaccurate map, in exchange for more memory storage.
Indeed, we can see from Euclidean geometry that the length of a curve can be approximated using straight lines that connecting various points on the curve. Although not the exact arc length of our curve, this approximation helps us to build ‘shortcuts’ where we sacrifice super precise representations of our maps/geometries in exchange for way more computational power. Of course, this trade-off must be balanced; we still need to accurately represent our maps to an audience and not risk losing too many data points from our simplification process.



Approximation of a Curve by Summing Straight Lines


This leads us into our first unary operator (works on a single geometry in isolation): Simplification.
Found in the sf package, our function of choice here is sf_simplify().
crumbs: Geospatial Data Science & Economic Spatial Models

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Seine Example
For example, we can see below how the sf_simplify() function reduces the complexity of the map of the rivers in France:

# st_simplify with 2000m 'measuring stick'
seine_simple <- st_simplify(seine, dTolerance = 2000) # 2000m



Show plotting code
# here we use the sf library to access the geom df `seine`

# original data
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=seine, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "Original Data") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

# simplified data
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=seine_simple, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "st_simplify()") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1 + p2









As we can see, after using st_simplify our graph has much less complexity, with fewer vertices. We can verify that it is computationally friendlier as a result:

# memory usage of og data
object.size(seine)

18096 bytes

# memory usage of simplified data
object.size(seine_simple)

9112 bytes


Note the makeup of the st_simplify function is very simple:
st_simplify(x = sfg, sfc, or sf object, preserveTopology = logical, dTolerance = numeric)
Where:

preserveTopology: logical, default is TRUE; asks whether to avoid invalid geometries (self-intersections, border crossings, etc). TRUE is much safer, more conservative; FALSE simplifies as much as possible, but allows for weird occurances in the geometry.
dTolerance: numeric; controls for how simplified we want our graph. Lower value corresponds to preserving the original geometry; higher values simplify the graphs more and more. Can think of this as the ‘length’ of our new measuring stick we want to use.

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
US States Example

# st_simplify polygons using 1000km 'measuring stick'
us_states_simple <- st_simplify(us_states, dTolerance = 100000) # 1000km

We can demonstrate this again, this time using polygons rather than linestrings.


Show plotting code
# plot 1: no change
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=us_states, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "Original Data") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

# plot 2: after st_simplify()
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=us_states_simple, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "st_simplify()") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1 + p2









Notice an issue here with this simplification: st_simplify simplifies objects on a per-geometry basis; i.e., it leads to overlapping and “holey” areal units, such as in our graph above.
A possible solution to this problem with polygons is to use other functions, such as ms_simplify() or smooth():

# ms_simplify()
us_states_ms_simple <- ms_simplify(us_states, keep=0.1, keep_shapes=TRUE)

# smooth()
us_states_smooth <- smooth(us_states, method = "ksmooth", smoothness = 6)



Show plotting code
# ms_simplify() plot
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=us_states_ms_simple, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "ms_simplify()") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

# smooth() plot
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=us_states_smooth, color = "black", linewidth=0.65) +
  labs(title = "smooth()") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1 + p2









Note that the smooth() function does not preserve topology similar to st_simplify(), but is useful when working with geometries that arise from spatially vectorizing a raster.

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Transforming
For example, to transform (shift) a map of New Zealand, we can simply add values to adjust the x and y-coordinates:

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# shift every geom value y-value by 100000m (1000km)
nz_shift_y <- nz.sfc + c(0,100000)
st_crs(nz_shift_y) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_shift_y.sf <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_shift_y) # assign new geoms back to og sf

# shift every geom value x-value by 50000m (500km)
nz_shift_x <- nz.sfc + c(50000,0)
st_crs(nz_shift_x) <- st_crs(nz) # set our trans geom to match our og CRS
nz_shift_x.sf <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_shift_x)



Show plotting code
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_shift_x.sf, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data=nz_shift_y.sf, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "TRANSFORMATION") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Scaling
Scaling our maps involves enlarging our shrinking objects by a factor. We can adjust these scales globally, to affect every point in our geometry; for example,

# shrink every geom value by 0.5
nz_global_center <- st_centroid(st_union(nz.sfc)) # GLOBAL center
nz_global_scale <- (nz.sfc - nz_global_center) * 0.5 + nz_global_center
st_crs(nz_global_scale) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_global_scale.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_global_scale)

Note that to get the global centroid, we need to take union of all our geometries using the st_union() function, after which we can apply to it st_centroid.


Show plotting code
p1<-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="gray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_global_scale.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  #geom_sf(data=nz_scale_inc.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "GLOBAL SCALING") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )


Or we can adjust these scales locally, treating geometries independently and requires points around which geometries are going to be scales (centroids, for example):

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# shrink every geom value y-value by 0.5
nz_centroid.sfc <- st_centroid(nz.sfc) # LOCAL centers
nz_scale <- (nz.sfc - nz_centroid.sfc) * 0.5 + nz_centroid.sfc
st_crs(nz_scale) <- st_crs(nz) 
nz_scale.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_scale)



Show plotting code
p2<-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_scale.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  #geom_sf(data=nz_scale_inc.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "LOCAL SCALING") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p1+p2

title: Class 03: Geometry Operations
text:
Rotation
Finally, we can rotate our graphs using a rotation matrix of the following form:
\[
R =
\begin{bmatrix}
  cos\theta & -sin\theta \\
  sin\theta & cos\theta
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Which rotates points in a clockwise direction. We can define a rotation function as the following:

rotation = function(degrees){
  r = degrees * pi / 180 #degrees to radians
  matrix(c(cos(r), sin(r), -sin(r), cos(r)), nrow=2, ncol=2)
}

We can implement this to rotate around selected points, such as centroids:

# extract geom column from nz sf object
nz.sfc <- st_geometry(nz)

# global rotation
nz_global_center <- st_centroid(st_union(nz.sfc)) # GLOBAL center
nz_rotate_global <- (nz.sfc - nz_global_center) * rotation(90) + nz_global_center
st_crs(nz_rotate_global) <- st_crs(nz)
nz_rotate_global.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_rotate_global)

# local rotations
nz_centroid.sfc <- st_centroid(nz.sfc) # centers we will shrink around locally (each region)
nz_rotate_local <- (nz.sfc - nz_centroid.sfc) * rotation(90) + nz_centroid.sfc
st_crs(nz_rotate_local) <- st_crs(nz) 
nz_rotate_local.sfc <- st_set_geometry(nz, nz_rotate_local)



Show plotting code
p1 <-ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_rotate_global.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="skyblue",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "GLOBAL ROTATION") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

p2<- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=nz, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill = "darkgray") +
  geom_sf(data=nz_rotate_local.sfc, color = "black", linewidth=0.65, fill="salmon",alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "LOCAL ROTATIONS") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5)
  )

title: Class 01: Intro to Vector Data & sf Library
text:
Basics
We have three basic geometries for our vector data: points, lines, & polygons
These geometries are stored as arrays: numeric vectors, matrices, & lists

Shapes

1. Points
Simplest form of geometry; typically translate to (LONG, LAT)
A single POINT is declared using the command st_point, by passing in a single numeric vector:

# single point
geom_point <- c(2,4)
single_pt <- st_point(geom_point)
st_as_text(single_pt)

[1] "POINT (2 4)"


whilst a collection of points is known as MULTIPOINT, declared using the command st_multipoint command, which expects a numeric matrix (specifically a 2D array):

# multiple points
geom_multipoints <- rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0))
multipts <- st_multipoint(geom_multipoints)
st_as_text(multipts)

[1] "MULTIPOINT ((2 4), (1 5), (0 2), (1 0))"




2. Lines
Lines are simply a collection of points connected sequentially (meaning the ordering of our points matters!)
A single LINESTRING can be constructed from a 2D numeric array, the same exact way as a MULTIPOINT, only now using the command st_linestring:

# single line
geom_multipoints <- rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0))
single_line <- st_linestring(geom_multipoints)
st_as_text(single_line)

[1] "LINESTRING (2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0)"


We can also construct multiple linestrings, known as MULTILINES using the command st_multilinestring: expects a list of numeric matrices (2D arrays).

# multiple lines
geom_multilines <- list(rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0)),
                        rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(2,2), c(3,3)),
                        rbind(c(1,1), c(1,0), c(1,-1)))
multi_lines <- st_multilinestring(geom_multilines)
st_as_text(multi_lines)

[1] "MULTILINESTRING ((2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0), (0 0, 1 1, 2 2, 3 3), (1 1, 1 0, 1 -1))"




3. Polygons
Finally, we can create shapes by building lines as we did before, but now making sure the first point & last point are the same. Polygons require a list of numeric array(s)
A single POLYGON follows the same logic as MULTILINES, now with the same coordinates for the first and last points. We use now the command st_polygon to build this object:

# single line
geom_singlepoly <- list(rbind(c(2,4), c(1,5), c(0,2), c(1,0), c(2,4)))
single_poly <- st_polygon(geom_singlepoly)
st_as_text(single_poly)

[1] "POLYGON ((2 4, 1 5, 0 2, 1 0, 2 4))"


We can, like before with lines, build & assign multiple POLYGONS to a single object, aptly named a MULTIPOLYGON. The difference for this is that we must input a list of lists; i.e. a list of single polygons, using the command st_multipolygon

# single line
geom_multipoly <- list(list(rbind(c(3,4), c(3,3), c(5,3), c(5,4), c(3,4))), # rectangle
                        list(rbind(c(1,4), c(1,5), c(2,4), c(1,4)))) # right triangle
multi_poly <- st_multipolygon(geom_multipoly)
st_as_text(multi_poly)

[1] "MULTIPOLYGON (((3 4, 3 3, 5 3, 5 4, 3 4)), ((1 4, 1 5, 2 4, 1 4)))"





Simple Features (sf)
SIMPLE FEATURE:

SF COLUMN (GEOMETRY + PROJECTION) +
ATTRIBUTE (DATA FRAME)

title: Class 01: Intro to Vector Data & sf Library
text:
Example 1: spatial geometries


Code
# multipoint (think: long-lat)
multipt_matrix <- rbind(c(3.2, 4), c( 4, 4.6), c(3.8, 4.4),
                           c(3.5, 3.8), c(3.4, 3.6), c(3.9, 4.5))
gm.multipt <- st_multipoint(multipt_matrix)

# linestring (connecting pts; order matters)
linestring_matrix <- rbind(c(0, 3), c(0,4), c(1,5), c(2,5))
gm.linestr <- st_linestring(linestring_matrix)

# polygon (last pt & first pt must match)
angle <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 100)
circle_coords <- cbind(3.5 + 0.5*cos(angle), 0.5 + 0.5*sin(angle))
polygon_matrix <- list(list(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,0), c(3,2), c(2,4), c(1,4), c(0,0))),
                       list(rbind(circle_coords, circle_coords[1,])))
gm.poly <- st_multipolygon(polygon_matrix)

# create these objects into a column: st_sfc
geom <- st_sfc(gm.multipt, gm.linestr, gm.poly)

# our normal (non-geom) dataframe
mock_data <- data.frame(objects = c('multipt', 'linestr', 'polyg'))

# append our geom data to our data_frame, declare it as a sf object
sf_mockdata <- st_sf(mock_data, geometry = geom)

# plot our shapes!
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=sf_mockdata, fill = "lavender") +
  theme_minimal()










Projections
The world is a 3D object: when we try to project this onto a 2D surface (like a map), it is impossible to not have distortion (proven by Gauss, known as the “Theorema Egregium” – reference for a deeper dive into the math).
The basic idea behind the differential geometry is that a (2D) plane has \(K=0\) Gaussian curvature, whilst a (3D) sphere w/ radius ‘R’ has a constant & strictly positive curvature, \(K=\frac{1}{R^2}\). There does not exist a function to perfectly map the plane to the sphere (and vice versa); consequentially, every cartographic projection must contain at least some distortion between distances.



Map Projection Distortion


Thus, we need to pay attention to what sort of projection structure our data has. There exists a plethora of ways to project the globe onto a map; what is important is that these projections are both:

well-defined, and
standardized (agree in their projections)

Otherwise when we try to build our spatial models, we might end up at completely incorrect coordinates. The ‘standard’ (most common) longitude-latitude used is Geodetic CRS: WGS 84; passed as an argument as crs = 'EPSG:4326'. For example:

gm.point <- st_point(c(11.3, 44.4)) # c(longitude,latitude)
gmc.point <- st_sfc(gm.point,
                    crs = 'EPSG:4326')
gmc.point; st_as_text(gmc.point)

Geometry set for 1 feature 
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 11.3 ymin: 44.4 xmax: 11.3 ymax: 44.4
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


[1] "POINT (11.3 44.4)"


What if we have an array (2D matrix) of multipoints that dont have a projection assigned to them? for example:

df.cities <- data.frame(
  name = c('Bologna', 'London', 'Madrid', 'Paris'),
  temperature = c(31, 21, 29,28),
  language = c('Italian', 'English', 'Spanish', 'French'),
  longitude = c(11.3,-0.1,-3.7,2.3),
  latitude = c(44.4,51.5, 40.4,48.8)
)
# Declare the data frame as an sf object, & declare our 'coords' col as the geometry
sf.cities <- st_as_sf(df.cities,
                      coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'))
sf.cities # Missing CRS!

Simple feature collection with 4 features and 3 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -3.7 ymin: 40.4 xmax: 11.3 ymax: 51.5
CRS:           NA
     name temperature language          geometry
1 Bologna          31  Italian POINT (11.3 44.4)
2  London          21  English POINT (-0.1 51.5)
3  Madrid          29  Spanish POINT (-3.7 40.4)
4   Paris          28   French  POINT (2.3 48.8)


Notice the output for CRS: NA – it is important to specify and/or standardize!

# Correct version
sf.cities <- st_as_sf(
  df.cities,
  coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'),
  crs = 'EPSG:4326'
  )

sf.cities

Simple feature collection with 4 features and 3 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -3.7 ymin: 40.4 xmax: 11.3 ymax: 51.5
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
     name temperature language          geometry
1 Bologna          31  Italian POINT (11.3 44.4)
2  London          21  English POINT (-0.1 51.5)
3  Madrid          29  Spanish POINT (-3.7 40.4)
4   Paris          28   French  POINT (2.3 48.8)



Note:



Columns
To store our geometry objects as a column in our dataframe, we use the command st_sfc
